title: Software squeezes more data out of Webb Telescope for imaging exoplanets
gist: Researchers built FLIP, which applies GPU-accelerated gradient descent (borrowed from neural network training) to tune a physical model of Webb's NIRCam and derive its point spread function in about half an hour. It raised exoplanet imaging signal-to-noise 1.5-2x, improved sensitivity 15x on one variable star, and found a planet at a CO2 wavelength for the first time (Nature, 2026).

themes.theme: AI optimization tools repurposed for physics modeling

insights.claim: Physics-based telescope models were previously computationally intractable because they contain too many parameters to tune, but gradient descent on GPUs, perfected for training large neural networks, now makes tuning them feasible.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: AI training infrastructure is spilling over into scientific computing, broadening demand for GPUs and differentiable programming tools.

insights.claim: FLIP (Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets) optimizes a physical model of the James Webb Space Telescope's NIRCam with what the article renders as 106 parameters, taking a bit more than half an hour on a current GPU, then fine-tunes on each science image.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Software can get significantly more out of existing scientific instruments without new hardware.

insights.claim: The researchers say FLIP could be modified to highlight where it makes the largest model changes, which may reveal what is happening with the telescope's hardware.

insights.claim: Using Webb data on HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani, FLIP boosted the signal-to-noise ratio by a factor of 1.5 to 2 and detected one of the planets at a carbon dioxide wavelength for the first time.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Better ability to characterize atmospheres increases the scientific return of Webb.

insights.claim: For TYC 5899, a star known to vary a lot between observations, FLIP boosted observational sensitivity by a factor of 15.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: The largest gains come for targets that are hardest to calibrate.

insights.claim: By lowering noise, FLIP should make it possible to detect dimmer, older, or lower-mass exoplanets that previously escaped detection.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: It widens the set of exoplanets that can be directly imaged, beyond young, hot giant planets.
